channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Colorado confirms foreign actors changed settings, silenced alarms and altered pumping at two small water systems
item.description: Colorado’s Governor’s office said on 18 September that foreign actors breached two small, privately owned drinking-water providers in late August, changing equipment settings, disabling alarms and remote access, and altering pumping cycles. The state says the disruptions were brief, the providers corrected them and alerted the state, and there was no known effect on treatment, water quality or public safety. The office cannot confirm which actors were involved, though it points to a known Iranian-backed campaign against water and wastewater systems; the FBI declined to comment, and Denver Water says its own systems were evaluated and are unaffected. As of 24 September nothing has moved: SecurityWeek’s 21 September and Industrial Cyber’s 22 September reports restate the same two-system disclosure, no third system has been reported, the utilities remain unnamed, and no CISA, EPA or WaterISAC statement specific to Colorado has appeared. Why this matters: the national campaign against internet-exposed water controllers now has hands-on process tampering confirmed by a state government rather than inferred. Each utility serves fewer than 200 people — and at that size, the alarm the intruders switched off is often the only operator on shift. - Colorado Governor’s office statement, reported by Reuters, AP, Axios Denver, the Denver Post, KRDO and SecurityWeek; context from CISA, FBI, EPA and NSA advisory AA26-097A - Intrusions late Aug 2026; disclosed 18 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek 21 Sep 2026 and Industrial Cyber 22 Sep 2026; no new development as of 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The Coast Guard cleared the boarded supertanker to resume trading — after finding evidence of a malicious actor aboard
item.category: Incident — confirmed malicious cyber activity aboard two US-bound tankers; no confirmed operational disruption; attribution unresolved
item.description: US Coast Guard and FBI personnel boarded two Texas-bound oil tankers in late August after indications that the vessels’ networks had been breached during the voyage. Rear Adm. Amy Grable, who commands Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News that reviewing the IT and other onboard systems of the Liberian-flagged crude carrier VL Prosperity did turn up evidence of a malicious cyber actor, but that nothing found suggested the ship was unsafe to operate. Iranian state media claims the intrusion reached the engine room — slowing coolant flow, raising engine speed, interfering with fuel delivery and cutting communications for about 30 hours — and those claims remain unverified; the Coast Guard has not attributed the incident to Iran. The vessel has since been cleared to resume normal operations, with a final investigation report still outstanding. The detail worth sitting with is Grable’s: this was one of an estimated 40–50 cyber missions the Coast Guard’s Cyber Protection Team carried out in the past year. - US Coast Guard Cyber Command via CBS News; Wall Street Journal; reported by SecurityWeek, The Record, Industrial Cyber, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and gCaptain - Boardings late Aug 2026; reported 15–18 Sep 2026; vessel cleared, reported 18–19 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A cyberattack stopped container handling at Tanjung Pelepas — and the restart ran on paper and manual gate-ins
item.category: Incident — confirmed cyberattack on terminal operating systems; container handling suspended at one of the world’s largest transhipment hubs
item.description: The Port of Tanjung Pelepas in Malaysia detected a cyber incident affecting its terminal operating systems late on 9 September and suspended container-handling operations as a precaution. A phased restart began the following day, with some export gate-ins processed manually while systems were recovered; the operator says container operations have since resumed. PTP is an MMC Group and APM Terminals joint venture that moved 14.03 million TEU in 2025, which puts it among the largest transhipment hubs anywhere. For OT defenders this is the cleanest recent example of the pattern that actually causes industrial downtime: the attack did not need to reach a crane PLC or a straddle carrier to stop the boxes moving — taking out the system that decides where every container goes was sufficient. - Port of Tanjung Pelepas spokesperson statement, reported by WorldCargo News - Incident detected 9 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A utility serving millions lost customer records through an internet-facing interface — and the energy side never noticed because it was never touched
item.category: Incident — confirmed data theft from an external-facing system at a major US electric and gas utility; energy delivery unaffected
item.description: CenterPoint Energy confirmed on 14 September that an unauthorised third party took customer data from one of its external-facing systems, after someone posted a data set on a criminal forum. The poster claims roughly 7.49 million records — names, phone numbers, billing addresses, account numbers and partial Social Security numbers — pulled through an interface the poster describes as having no authentication token, no rate limiting and no web application firewall. CenterPoint has not confirmed the figure or the authenticity of the published set, and says energy services were unaffected and no material financial impact is expected; class-action suits have already been filed. For OT readers the value here is not the breach itself but the asset class: a customer-facing interface at a utility, outside the CIP perimeter, invisible to the OT asset inventory and owned by nobody in the control room. - CenterPoint Energy statement and SEC filing, reported by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek and Security Affairs - Confirmed 14 Sep 2026; reported 16 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A source-code server was the way in and an SSH key named “backdoor” the way back — and two of the eleven victims build or run energy and SCADA systems
item.category: Threat activity — Acronis TRU: PRC-linked cluster “Red Heron” exploiting Gitea CVE-2026-60004 (CVSS 9.8); 11 confirmed compromises in five countries, including a renewable-energy company and a SCADA/HMI tool maker
item.description: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit reported on 13 September that a cluster it tracks as Red Heron has been exploiting CVE-2026-60004, a CVSS 9.8 remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea source-code platform (versions 1.17 through 1.27.0; fixed in 1.27.1 on 27 July), and confirms 11 compromised organisations in five countries: Canada, Argentina, Taiwan, the United States and Sri Lanka. Two victims are why it is on this page: a Canadian renewable-energy company, where the actor took source code, credentials and secrets and planted its own SSH keys, and a Taiwanese maker of SCADA and HMI tools, whose repositories were taken. After exploitation the actor adds SSH authorised keys with names such as “-backdoor” and “root-shell”, and installs an LD_PRELOAD rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT to hide its processes. Acronis attributes the activity with moderate confidence to a PRC-linked context; that is a vendor assessment, not a government attribution, and nothing in the report says a process was touched. What was taken is what you would want if you meant to come back — and, in the vendor case, what you would want if you meant to reach that vendor’s customers. - Acronis Threat Research Unit analysis (primary); reported by The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber; GreyNoise overlap inference noted separately - Gitea fix 27 Jul 2026; Acronis report 13 Sep 2026; GreyNoise inference 21 Sep 2026 — verified 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Only 13% of the network segments that contain OT devices hold nothing but OT — and oil and gas has one of the biggest blast radii
item.category: Research — Forescout Vedere Labs: segmentation analysis of 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices across 209 organisations
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published an analysis on 22 September of 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices at 209 organisations. Only 13% of segments that contain OT devices are OT-only; nearly half of them also hold IT and IoT devices, with UPS units, building automation controllers and PLCs commonly found alongside ordinary IT equipment. Oil and gas ranks with business services and healthcare for the largest average “blast radius” — how much an attacker can reach from one foothold. Utilities score lower than oil and gas, but Forescout notes that does not mean they are adequately segmented. Why it matters: almost every OT-impacting incident on this page began on the IT side, and a mixed segment is where the IT-to-OT step costs an attacker nothing. - Forescout Vedere Labs research; reported by SecurityWeek - Published 22 Sep 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] ENISA’s annual report puts a Chinese espionage group inside European shipping — through phishing, USB sticks and edge routers
item.category: Threat landscape — ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 (covering 2025): China-nexus Mustang Panda espionage against maritime organisations in at least seven EU member states; espionage, no disruption described
item.description: ENISA published its Threat Landscape 2026 on 23 September, covering calendar year 2025. It names the China-nexus group Mustang Panda (also tracked as Earth Preta) as running cyber-espionage against maritime organisations in at least seven EU member states, using spear-phishing, infected USB drives, PlugX malware variants and compromised edge routers that serve both to steal information and as relay points. Across the EU the report counts 4,709 hacktivist campaigns, 89% of them DDoS, and attributes 47.6% of state-nexus activity to Russia-nexus actors. No disruption of vessel or port operations is described. Why it matters to OT: the methods are exactly the ones that reach ship and terminal systems — a USB stick carried aboard and an unpatched router at the edge — and espionage access is the stage before any disruptive option. - ENISA Threat Landscape 2026; reported by Splash247, Politico Europe and Industrial Cyber - Published 23 Sep 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Twelve flaws in a Siemens edge processing box chain to root — the device that sits between your PROFINET segment and everything else
item.category: Research — Nozomi Networks Labs: 12 vulnerabilities in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 local processing engine; chainable to root
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its research on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 Local Processing Engine, identifying twelve vulnerabilities in firmware below V4.0 HF0, with three more affecting other configurations including the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client. The reported issue classes cover privilege escalation, path traversal, authentication bypass, command injection and buffer overflows, several of which chain to root-level control — which on this class of device means telemetry manipulation, alarm suppression and a foothold for attacks against the OT network behind it. Siemens has no fix for some of the findings; the published workarounds are restricting access and disabling the PROFINET DCP service. One presentational note: the identifiers attached to this research are 2025-series CVEs appearing in a September 2026 write-up, which is legitimate — Siemens and CISA advisory activity for this device dates back to 2025 — but it means part of this is a fuller public account of older findings rather than wholly new disclosure. Check the identifiers against Siemens ProductCERT before raising a change record. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, reported by Industrial Cyber; verify identifiers against Siemens ProductCERT - Published 18 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Check Point confirms two exploited flaws at once — the VPN gateway that fronts the plant, and the management server that writes its rules
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-85102 (Security Gateway and Spark VPN, CVSS 9.8) and CVE-2026-93616 (Security Management Server, CVSS 9.8), Check Point; both exploited in the wild; added to CISA KEV 22 Sep 2026, federal deadline 25 Sep 2026
item.description: Check Point said on 22 September that CVE-2026-85102 — improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls, allowing unauthenticated remote code execution — has been exploited since 12 September, three days after its 9 September patch, in what the vendor calls a wave of attempts against Spark customers. In the same advisory it disclosed CVE-2026-93616, a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that allows script execution and Java class loading; the fix shipped on 22 September, after what Check Point describes as a handful of pinpointed attacks on 23 July, so it was a zero-day for about two months. CISA added both to the KEV catalogue on 22 September with a 25 September deadline. Neither is attributed and no victim count is given. The management flaw is a different bug from CVE-2026-91843, the unexploited management-server flaw disclosed on 17 September. Why it matters to OT: Check Point gateways are a common IT/OT boundary and remote-site firewall, Spark appliances sit in small unmanned sites, and the management server holds the policy for every boundary it administers — so whoever owns it can open the path into the plant. - Check Point security advisory (22 Sep 2026) and CISA KEV alert (22 Sep 2026); reported by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek, The Hacker News, Help Net Security and SecurityAffairs - Gateway fix 9 Sep 2026; exploitation from 12 Sep 2026 (gateway) and 23 Jul 2026 (management); management fix and KEV addition 22 Sep 2026; federal deadline 25 Sep 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The box that decides which VLAN a device lands in can be taken by an unauthenticated request — and it is being taken
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-76460, CVSS 10.0, Cisco Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC; exploited as a zero-day, no workaround, in KEV
item.description: Cisco disclosed a maximum-severity authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and the ISE Passive Identity Connector, tracked as CVE-2026-76460 at CVSS 10.0, caused by insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the web management interface and gain unauthorised access to the device. Cisco says it was exploited as a zero-day; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September, now passed. There is no workaround — upgrading is the only remediation, with fixes in ISE 3.5 P4, 3.4 P7, 3.3 P12, 3.2 P11 and 3.1 P12. For industrial sites, ISE is frequently the thing enforcing which devices land on which VLAN, including the boundary between enterprise and plant. Whoever holds ISE can rewrite that boundary without touching a switch, a firewall or a controller. Since then: Cisco’s advisory remains at its 16 September revision with exploitation confirmed but no attribution, ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and must be migrated, and Singapore’s CSA issued its own alert on 21 September. It is the second exploited Cisco management plane this month: CVE-2026-20079 in Secure Firewall Management Center (KEV 9 September, deadline 12 September, passed) is being used by three clusters Talos tracks — a state-sponsored group dropping JSP web shells, a second whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s and which deployed Cyclops Blink, and a Qilin ransomware operator. Cisco replaced the FMC hot fixes with hardening releases on 16 September (7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2, 10.1.0); the companion static-credential flaw CVE-2026-20316 is not in KEV. - Cisco security advisories (ISE and FMC), Cisco Talos, CSA Singapore alert AL-2026-126 and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, reported by SecurityWeek, CyberScoop, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Disclosed and added to KEV 16 Sep 2026; federal deadline 19 Sep 2026, now passed; FMC context from Cisco advisory rev 2.6 (16 Sep 2026) and Cisco Talos (updated 21 Sep 2026) — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The SD-WAN orchestrator that pushes configuration to every remote site is being exploited — and two of its four release trains have no fix yet
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-93952, CVSS v3.1 10.0 / v4.0 9.5, Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (on-premises); exploited in the wild; added to CISA KEV 22 Sep 2026, federal deadline 25 Sep 2026
item.description: Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on 22 September for CVE-2026-93952, an input-validation flaw (CWE-20) in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator that lets a remote attacker reach privileged internal functionality and impact the orchestrator host, and said it “is known to be actively exploited”. Exploitation requires certificate-based authentication between VeloCloud Edges and the orchestrator to be configured and network access to the orchestrator’s web interface; no tenant or operator credentials are needed. Affected are 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier; fixed releases are 5.2.3.16 and 6.4.2.8 or later, and Arista lists no fixed release yet for the 6.1.x or 7.0.x trains. CISA added the flaw to KEV the same day with a 25 September deadline. Why it matters to OT: SD-WAN is how many utilities, pipelines and multi-site manufacturers connect substations, pump stations, compressor sites and branch plants, and the orchestrator is the one system that configures every one of those edges at once. - Arista Security Advisory 0183 and CISA KEV alert (22 Sep 2026); reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory and KEV addition 22 Sep 2026; federal deadline 25 Sep 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A small-office switch flaw patched in June is now in KEV — GreyNoise counts 996 compromised switches, more than half still on factory-default credentials
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-7273, Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches; unauthenticated LAN-side command execution; exploited in the wild; added to CISA KEV 21 Sep 2026, federal deadline 24 Sep 2026
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 21 September with a 24 September federal deadline. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker with LAN access to the management interface execute operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request; Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and per-model equivalents, and publishes no CVSS score. GreyNoise’s report the same day documents what it describes as the first in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor it assesses as a Chinese speaker, active since 7 May, exploited 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries — Italy, the United States and Taiwan lead — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were using factory-default credentials. The same actor exploited two WordPress flaws to steal government records and has targeted UniFi OS, Gitea, Proxmox VE and PAN-OS GlobalProtect. GreyNoise infers an overlap with Red Heron from shared infrastructure and malware; that is an inference. Why it matters to OT: GS1900 is exactly the class of cheap managed switch that ends up in a pump house, a remote substation cabinet or a machine-builder’s control panel, and a switch configuration is a map of the network behind it. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, Zyxel security advisory (16 Jun 2026) and GreyNoise research - Zyxel advisory 16 Jun 2026; KEV addition and GreyNoise report 21 Sep 2026; federal deadline 24 Sep 2026 — verified 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A 9.8 in the MQTT client of a TCP/IP stack embedded in countless controllers — and the affected-products list is whoever compiled it in
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-265-01: CVE-2026-87121, CVSS v3.1 9.8, out-of-bounds write in the lwIP TCP/IP stack MQTT client; plus ICSA-26-265-02, a double free in lwIP; no confirmed exploitation
item.description: CISA published two advisories on 22 September for lwIP, the open-source lightweight TCP/IP stack found inside a large share of embedded devices. ICSA-26-265-01 covers CVE-2026-87121, an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client application that may allow an attacker to gain full code execution on the device; it scores 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 — network-reachable, low complexity, no privileges and no user interaction — and was reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay. ICSA-26-265-02 covers a separate double-free flaw in lwIP reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security. No exploitation has been reported. The difficulty for defenders is that lwIP is a library, not a product: whether a given PLC, I/O module, gateway or sensor is exposed depends on whether its maker compiled in the MQTT client, and downstream vendor advisories have not yet appeared. Ubuntu’s tracker still listed its lwip packages as “needs evaluation” on 24 September. Why it matters to OT: MQTT is the protocol of choice for pushing plant telemetry to brokers and cloud platforms, so the devices most likely to carry this client are the ones deliberately connected outward. - CISA advisories ICSA-26-265-01 and ICSA-26-265-02 (22 Sep 2026), corroborated by the CVE record via the Ubuntu security tracker and Chemical Facility Security News - Published 22 Sep 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA pushed Siemens’ September building-automation and physical-security flaws to US operators — and the Desigo CC one still has no patch
item.category: Advisory — CISA republication of Siemens advisories, 22 Sep 2026: Siveillance Control and Control Pro CVE-2026-50093 (CVSS 9.0, fixed) and Desigo CC family CVE-2026-34223 (CVSS 8.2, no fix); plus SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT and WTV676/WTV776; no confirmed exploitation
item.description: CISA republished a batch of Siemens advisories on 22 September that Siemens first released on 8 September. ICSA-26-265-03 covers CVE-2026-50093 in Siveillance Control and Siveillance Control Pro: the OIS web module allows arbitrary file upload to the server, which can lead to root access and compromise of the whole OIS environment; it scores 9.0 (8.9 under CVSS v4.0) and is fixed in Siveillance Control V3.0.22.2177 and V4.0.11.2177 and Control Pro V3.0.12.2173 and V4.0.9.2178. ICSA-26-265-05 covers CVE-2026-34223 in the Desigo CC family, reported by Michelin CERT: a script embedded in a malicious user-defined graphics document runs on the client when the document is opened and can write arbitrary files to the client’s operating system. It scores 8.2, needs local access and a user to open the file, affects all versions of the Desigo CC ClickOnce, Flex and Installed Clients V6–V7 and Desigo CC V8–V9, and has no fix. The same batch republished a path traversal in SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT and an input-validation flaw in WTV676/WTV776. No exploitation is reported. Why it matters to OT: Desigo CC runs building management — HVAC, fire and electrical monitoring — in plants, data centres, hospitals and airports, and Siveillance Control is the command layer over access control and video. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-265-03, -05, -07 and -08 republishing Siemens ProductCERT advisories; CVE records; review by Chemical Facility Security News - Siemens advisories 8 Sep 2026; CISA republication 22 Sep 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The VPN client on the machine builder’s laptop can be made to run commands as root — and the injected setting survives a reboot
item.category: Advisory — CERT@VDE VDE-2026-089: CVE-2026-75925, CVSS v3.1 9.6, CRLF injection in the IXON VPN Client before 1.4.7, used with the Lenze x500 IoT Gateway; no confirmed exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-089 on 21 September for CVE-2026-75925, a CRLF injection in the IXON VPN Client before version 1.4.7, the remote-access client used with the Lenze x500 IoT Gateway. An attacker can inject settings that make the client run commands with root or SYSTEM privileges; the client’s configuration interface performs no authentication check, and the injected settings persist across restarts. The score is 9.6 under CVSS v3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C), so a user action is needed. The fix is version 1.4.7, and the IXON cloud already blocks older clients from connecting. No exploitation has been reported. Why it matters to OT: this client lives on the engineering laptops of machine builders and integrators who maintain customer equipment remotely, and a root-level foothold on that laptop sits at the start of a tunnel that ends inside your plant. - CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-089 (Lenze / IXON) - Published 21 Sep 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Twenty-two flaws in the IO-Link master that talks to your sensors — two of them unauthenticated to root, and the same firmware ships under three brand names
item.category: Advisory — CERT@VDE VDE-2026-014: 22 CVEs in Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link masters, two at CVSS 9.8; same firmware in Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 (VDE-2026-027) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212/YN115 (VDE-2026-028); no known exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September: Pepperl+Fuchs has fixed 22 vulnerabilities, found by Nozomi Networks researchers Gabriele Quagliarella and Luca Borzacchiello, in the firmware of its ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules — the DIN-rail devices that bridge IO-Link sensors and actuators onto PROFINET or EtherNet/IP. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-27565, an unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, also 9.8. Most of the remainder (CVE-2026-27547 through -27564) are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that reach root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557 (7.5) is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the SSH server’s private keys and CVE-2026-27553 (6.5) discloses password hashes. Affected firmware is below 1.7.4 and the fix is 1.7.8. Because the firmware is shared, the same flaws ship in rebadged units: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 (VDE-2026-027, 20 CVEs, same fix) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 (VDE-2026-028). No exploitation has been reported and no CISA advisory had appeared as of this edition. The device sits at the last hop before the physical sensor, which makes it both the least-inventoried thing on the line and the one whose readings everything upstream believes. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-014, VDE-2026-027 and VDE-2026-028; CVE records; Nozomi Networks Labs research listing - Published 16 Sep 2026 — verified 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Rockwell has now revised its “what to do when someone else set the PLC password” notice five times — and this week it added the Micro800 family
item.category: Guidance — Rockwell Automation SD1790 revision 5.0: hardening and password-recovery instructions extended to Micro820 and Micro850, after FBI-reported attackers set passwords on exposed PLCs and locked operators out; no CVE
item.description: Rockwell Automation issued revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790 on 18 September, extending its hardening guidance and its instructions for restoring access to a controller whose password is unknown to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers, alongside the MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 the notice originally covered when it was first published on 30 July. The premise has not changed: the notice references the FBI’s 30 July public service announcement describing attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none existed, so that operators lose access to their own controllers. There is no CVE, because there is no vulnerability — the access path is a controller reachable from the internet with no password. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data; what it adds is scope. The Micro800 family is the entry-level PLC sold through distribution to small machine builders, water systems and building plants, which are precisely the sites least likely to have read revision 1.0. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790 revision 5.0; FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026 as referenced by the notice - Original 30 Jul 2026; revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026 — verified 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] NIST’s OT security guide is being rebuilt around CSF 2.0 and zero trust — and you have until 30 November to say what will not work in a plant
item.description: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, on 21 September, with comments due by 30 November. The draft is restructured around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with stronger alignment to risk management and zero-trust principles, expanded implementation guidance on asset management and network monitoring, and new security architecture recommendations. Its scope widens to building automation and control systems, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and IIoT and cloud convergence. Industrial Cyber’s review describes a 321-page document that calls a mature OT defence “consequence-driven”, recommends separating OT from enterprise networks, and describes privileged access management as “the clearest expression of zero trust” in OT. It is guidance, not regulation, but SP 800-82 is the reference many OT security programmes are built on, so the final text will shape audits and procurement. - NIST Computer Security Resource Center; review by Industrial Cyber - Draft published 21 Sep 2026; comments due 30 Nov 2026 — verified 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six national agencies published the Active Directory playbook — and for most plants that directory is the shortest route from the office to the control room
item.category: Guidance — ASD, CISA, NSA, CCCS, NCSC-NZ and NCSC-UK: detecting and mitigating 17 Active Directory compromise techniques
item.description: Six national cyber agencies — Australia’s ASD, CISA, NSA, Canada’s CCCS, New Zealand’s NCSC and the UK’s NCSC — published joint guidance on 16 September covering the seventeen techniques adversaries most commonly use to compromise Microsoft Active Directory, with detection methods and hardening recommendations for each. The list runs from Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting and password spraying through unconstrained delegation, AD Certificate Services abuse, DCSync and NTDS.dit extraction to golden and silver tickets, golden SAML, Entra Connect compromise, SID history abuse and shadow credentials. There is nothing OT-specific in it, which is exactly why it belongs on this page: in most plants the engineering workstations, historians and HMIs are domain-joined, and every OT-impacting ransomware case on this dashboard ran through identity rather than through an industrial protocol. - Joint guidance from ASD, CISA, NSA, CCCS, NCSC-NZ and NCSC-UK, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 16 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026
